brief.market_summary: This is sample content for previewing the layout, not real market data. Equity futures point higher, led by semiconductors, while 10-year yields drift lower after a soft inflation print. Brent is heading for a weekly loss on OPEC+ supply signals, and large-cap crypto is firm on steady ETF inflows.
brief.since_last: Sample: the market moved from pricing a pause to roughly even odds of a December cut, which pulled the 10-year down 3bp and lifted rate-sensitive growth stocks. Oil lost its geopolitical premium.

brief.instructor_take: Sample, for layout only. Here's how I read this morning: the market is trading one variable, the path of Fed cuts, and yesterday's soft core PCE moved it. When inflation surprises low, I look first at the 2-year yield because it reacts most directly to policy expectations, then at long-duration assets that benefit. That's why two of my three ideas lean on lower yields. What a newer investor might miss is that the same data hurt energy: lower rates don't help oil when supply is rising. I'd be wrong if Friday's sentiment survey shows inflation expectations jumping, so I'd size modestly ahead of it.

top_ideas.title: Add duration while cut odds rebuild
top_ideas.one_liner: Soft PCE reopens Dec cut; 10Y has room toward 3.9%
top_ideas.thesis: Sample idea for layout only. Soft core PCE revives December cut odds; intermediate Treasuries offer carry plus upside if yields keep falling.
top_ideas.reasoning: Sample. I start from the data: core PCE came in at 0.1% against 0.2% expected, and that's the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. When the inflation input to the Fed's reaction function softens, cut odds rise, and intermediate Treasuries like IEF gain as yields fall. I prefer IEF to TLT because the 7-10 year part of the curve moves with cut expectations without as much long-end supply risk. I'd change my mind if the 10-year closed above 4.25%, because that would mean the market is pricing something other than cuts.

top_ideas.title: Semis on guidance momentum
top_ideas.one_liner: Foundry beat extends AI capex cycle; buy dips
top_ideas.thesis: Sample idea for layout only. A foundry beat and raised guide extend the AI capex cycle into big-tech earnings.
top_ideas.reasoning: Sample. TSMC's beat and raised guide is the most direct read on AI chip demand, since it manufactures for nearly every major designer. Strong foundry guidance tends to feed through to the whole group via estimate revisions, which I think is the most reliable driver of semis over weeks. Lower yields help too, because semis are long-duration growth assets. The risk a newer investor might miss is crowding: after a 6% month, buy pullbacks rather than chase.

top_ideas.title: Lighten energy into OPEC+ supply
top_ideas.one_liner: Brent losing premium as OPEC+ adds barrels; trim XLE
top_ideas.thesis: Sample idea for layout only. OPEC+ supply signals outweigh the macro tailwind for crude; energy stocks lag.
top_ideas.reasoning: Sample. Oil is caught between two forces: lower yields and a weaker dollar should help, but OPEC+ signalling more barrels dominates. Supply news usually beats macro for crude over weeks. Exxon's report on Friday is the next test of whether lower prices are eating into buybacks, which is what supports energy stocks. I'd be wrong if Brent reclaims $76, which would suggest a supply disruption I'm not seeing.

lesson.explanation: Sample: a bull steepener is when yields fall across the curve but short-term yields fall more than long-term ones. It usually happens when markets start pricing rate cuts. Short maturities track the Fed closely, while long maturities also carry inflation and supply risk.
lesson.todays_example: Sample: today the 10-year fell 3bp and the 2-year only 2bp, so the curve actually flattened slightly. That's a bull flattener, the opposite case. A true bull steepener needs the front end to lead, which is what to watch if cut odds keep rising.
